flawed_step: Step 4: the general construction only works when n ≡ 0 or 1 (mod 4). For n = 6 (and any n ≡ 2 or 3 mod 4), n(n-1)/2 is odd, so no graph can have exactly half of the possible edges.
counterexample: n = 6: K6 has 15 edges. If G ≅ complement(G), then |E(G)| = |E(complement)| and together they add up to 15, so |E(G)| = 7.5. That is impossible, so no self-complementary graph on 6 vertices exists.
assessment_summary:
Proof attempt:
1. Let G be a simple graph on n vertices with complement G'. Then E(G) and E(G') split the edges of K_n, so |E(G)| + |E(G')| = n(n-1)/2. — Justified: this follows from the definition of the complement.
2. If G ≅ G', then |E(G)| = |E(G')|, so |E(G)| = n(n-1)/4. — Justified: an isomorphism keeps the number of edges the same.
3. So a self-complementary graph on n vertices can only exist if 4 divides n(n-1), which happens exactly when n ≡ 0 or 1 (mod 4). — Justified: n and n-1 have opposite parity, so 4 must divide whichever one is even.
4. To prove the claim for every n ≥ 4, we would build a self-complementary graph for each n. For n ≡ 0 (mod 4), split the vertices into four blocks A, B, C, D of size n/4. Make A and D cliques, join A–B, B–C and C–D completely, and put no other edges. For n ≡ 1 (mod 4), add one vertex joined to A and D. These graphs work. But n = 6 is neither 0 nor 1 mod 4, and no construction can cover it. — NOT justified: by Steps 1–3, n = 6 gives 15 total edges, so we would need 7.5 edges. That rules out every n ≡ 2 or 3 (mod 4), such as 6, 7, 10 and 11.
5. Conclusion: a self-complementary graph exists for every n ≥ 4. — Not justified: it depends on Step 4, which fails, and Steps 1–3 actually disprove it.
Verdict: The statement is false. At n = 6 (which is ≥ 4), no self-complementary graph exists, because such a graph would need 15/2 edges. This is exactly the kind of refutation the definitions ask for.
